problem:
The intersection of the planes $-x+y-2z=0$ and $-x-2y+z-3=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{2},0⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$
worked_solution:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this to the first equation gives

$$
-x+y-2(0)=0\,⟹\,x=y,
$$

and substituting $z=0$ and $x=y$ into the second equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-x-2y+z-3 & =0 \\ -y-2y+0-3 & =0 \\ -3y & =3 \\ y & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=y=-1$ and $a=⟨-1,-1,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $-x+y-2z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨-1,1,-2⟩.$

- For the plane $-x-2y+z-3=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨-1,-2,1⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨-1,1,-2⟩\times ⟨-1,-2,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-3i+3j+3k \\  & =⟨-3,3,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can pick any vector that is parallel to ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}$ as a direction vector of the line. So, let 

$$
b=\frac{1}{3}({n}_{1}\times {n}_{2})=⟨-1,1,1⟩.
$$

The equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨-1,-1,0⟩+t⟨-1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=-1-1=-2,$ and $b=⟨-1,1,1⟩.$
